pl-l3d23c8-d1e112.summary: Exegesis of Hebrews 11:1: faith is the substance of things hoped for because through it those things subsist in us now and will subsist in the future by experience; it is the proof and conviction of the non-apparent because, when doubted, they are proved by faith (as the future resurrection by the faith of the patriarchs), or because it proves that non-apparent things exist. Properly, faith is the substance of hoped-for things because it underlies them as the unchangeable foundation of goods.
claims: Hoped-for goods subsist in us through faith and will subsist in fact later.
Faith proves non-apparent things to the doubter.
Faith is properly the substance of hoped-for things because it is their foundation.

pl-l3d23c8-d1e127.summary: Asks whether the description also fits hope. Either answer may be granted: if it fits hope, faith and hope differ in other respects; but it may fittingly be said to fit faith alone, since faith alone is called the foundation, not because the virtue of faith can exist without hope and charity.
claims: Whether the Hebrews description fits hope may be answered either way.
Faith alone is called the foundation.
Faith as a virtue does not exist without hope and charity.

pl-l3d23c8-d1e130.summary: Augustine confirms the interdependence: faith working through love cannot be without hope, nor love without hope, nor hope without love, nor both without faith; faith without love profits nothing.
claims: Formed faith, hope, and love are mutually inseparable.

pl-l3d23c8-d1e148.summary: Something can be believed that is not hoped for, but nothing hoped for that is not believed; therefore the act of believing naturally precedes the act of hoping. Scripture's placing of faith before hope refers to this natural priority of acts, not to a temporal or causal priority of the virtues, though some also grant a natural (not temporal) priority of the virtue of faith over hope.
claims: Everything hoped for is believed, but not everything believed is hoped for.
The act of faith naturally precedes the act of hope.
The virtue of faith does not precede the virtue of hope in time or as cause.
Some grant a natural priority of the virtue of faith over hope.

pl-l3d23c8.summary: Expounds Hebrews 11:1 as a description of faith: faith is the 'substance of things hoped for' because hoped-for goods subsist in us through it now and will subsist by experience later, and because it underlies them as their unchangeable foundation; it is the 'argument' of the non-apparent because it proves them. The description can be applied to hope or reserved to faith alone; faith-as-virtue never exists without hope and charity, but the act of believing naturally, not temporally, precedes the act of hoping.
claims: Faith is the substance of things hoped for because it makes them subsist in us and underlies them as foundation.
Faith is the proof and conviction of the non-apparent.
The Hebrews description may be applied to hope, but is more properly reserved to faith as foundation.
Formed faith, hope, and charity cannot exist without one another.
One can believe without hoping, but cannot hope for what one does not believe.
The act of faith naturally, not temporally or causally, precedes the act of hope.
